Saskatoon's water conservation strategy provides a roadmap of actions that will help reduce water use in the community and in the city's own
operations.
Today's presentation will provide background on water use in Saskatoon and why we need a water conservation strategy.
It outlines our water conservation targets and finally summarizes the actions that are required to meet those targets.
Like to begin by paying respects to the first nations and matey ancestors who for thousands of years cared for the land and water that sustains us.
Through the strategy we take responsibility to care for the shared water system that will support the needs and well-being of both present and future generations.
Saskatoon residents, businesses and institutions use 40 billion liters of water per year with half of its half of it used by residents.
In Saskatoon, total water use has remained constant despite a growing population and economy per capita consumption has trend of downward.
All this is good news are efforts to conserve water.
We can build on the many positive processes already underway.
However, we continue to have high summer peaks and in the summer months water used doubles.
The demand for water in the summer may intensify with climate change.
In addition, aging infrastructure continues to pose a risk to our water treatment system and our ability to provide safe and reliable water to Saskatoon.
Concerving water has many benefits and can help alleviate those risks posed by climate change in aging infrastructure.
Water conservation can help ensure we meet the communities needs in the long term even with a growing population.
The strategy recognizes four main reasons for conserving water.
First to help households and businesses moderate their water use and reduce the utility burden faced by those most impacted by costs.
By placing equity and opportunity at the forefront of program planning.
We can make our programs accessible to a broad audience and benefit those that need it the most.
Second, we need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and meet low emissions community plan targets.
The emissions related to treating and pumping water make up a third of overall city emissions.
Third, conservation helps increase water system resiliency and prepare for changing climate projections show that our current pace of greenhouse gas emissions.
Saskatoon will have doubled the number of days 25 degrees or more and 6 times the number of days at 30 degrees.
This will result in increased outdoor water use in higher costs reducing water use can help us prepare for less predictable precipitation less dependable water flows and more frequent droughts.
And fourth to help manage water demand to ease strains on the city's water system, especially during those summer peak periods.
We can ease strain on our capacity limited water system and create opportunities to better manage and schedule capital expenditures potentially differing or reducing spending.

The conservation targets were set in the low emissions community plan action 25 is a 5% reduction in absolutely water demand by 2026 and action 26 is a 20% outdoor and 30% indoor water use reduction by 2050.

The initiatives were chosen and prioritized based on overall water and greenhouse gas reduces reduced with specific focus on peak demand reductions as well as the cost and savings associated with the measures.
The chart on the graph which can be found on page 32 of the strategy shows the costs and savings to the city for each initiative for each unit of water saved.

The initiatives with bars below the x-axis indicate the city will save money with water reductions with water bars indicating bigger reductions while the bars above the x-axis are those that will cost money to implement.

The previous slide focused on costs and savings to the city however many programs will also result in savings to the public programs that support utility affordability and tailor conservation to lower moderate income households or those experiencing energy poverty were highly prioritized.
As were programs that had strong public preference so the table on the slide here shows the top programs that were preferred by the public and industry stakeholders who engaged.
The strategy describes 31 opportunities across the residential commercial and civic sectors that will help mitigate risks and manage water demand.
The water actions can together meet the low emissions plan targets.
Implementation of water conservation near term priorities which were also identified in the water conservation strategy update report from September of 2021 have begun and are listed on the slide.

The full phased action plan is available on page 47 and 48 of the strategy includes things like residential toilet and shower head rebates commercial audits and fixture replacement incentives residential commercial irrigation upgrade incentives and more civic water conservation.
These initiatives will be brought forward for funding and approval as implementation planning continues.
The strategy provides guidance for future work planning to help consider the cost and benefits of conservation alongside other water system investment considerations.
